newsitem.title: UK: Bank ratings on downward slope, but no panic yet.
newsitem.headline: Bank ratings on downward slope, but no panic yet.

text.p: The creditworthiness of banks has been on a downward slope for years as fierce competition has taken its toll, but rating agency experts say the trend is not a cause for alarm.

Deutsche Bank, one of only three banks rated triple-A by the top credit agencies, is the latest bank to come under the spotlight amid troubles at its London-based fund management arm, Morgan Grenfell Asset Management (MGAM).

While there is speculation that Deutsche could lose its coveted top grade -- some can envision a world with no triple-A banks left at all -- credit analysts say the trend reflects a more vibrant banking market, even if more dangerous.
"The trend for the future is increasing stress in the world banking market," said Samuel Theodore, managing director for European financial institutions at Moody's Investors Service in London.
"Banks need to generate more profits, while at the same time they are coping with overcapacity," he said. "Banks at the margin are at more risk than in the past."
Greg Root, president of Thomson BankWatch in New York, said the nature of banking has changed but that did not mean the institutions were that much more risky.

"I don't necessary think that banks as a whole have weakened over the last 10 years," he said. "It has been a change in the mix of the business which doesn't necessarily mean a lesser quality in the business from a credit standpoint."
Root said there had been a general strengthening of bank capital and banks had become better at identifying, monitoring and controlling risk.

"We're generally more comfortable with the banking industry than our peers," he said. "The business has changed dramatically from a lending business to one where they're much more involved with financial transactions."
According to data from European rating agency IBCA, Moody's had 23 commercial banks with triple-A ratings in 1989. It now has four.
Standard & Poor's total has fallen to three from 10 and IBCA's has dropped to six from nine, the data showed.
Other than Deutsche, only Rabobank Nederland BA and Union Bank of Switzerland have triple-A grades from both Moody's and S&P. J.P. Morgan and Co is rated AAA by IBCA and S&P but not by Moody's.

"The world is more competitive. Business cycles are shorter. Virtually every industry is getting less stable," said IBCA managing director Robin Monro-Davies. But he added: "Moody's has been much more violent than S&P and ourselves."

Monro-Davies said he did not expect the trend to continue and he saw no reason why there should be no triple-A rated banks left. "It (the general downgrading) has reached a reasonable level now," he said.
Theodore at Moody's said it was possible a day could come when there were no more triple-A banks.

"But I'm not sure that is the most essential characteristic in today's banking market," he said. "A bank can maintain its key creditworthiness and at the same time be in a more dynamic market which would make us perhaps put AA on it."
The "dynamic" nature of the market for Deutsche Bank has been an issue for analysts.

Moody's in July revised its outlook on the German banking giant down to negative from stable. Moody's said at the time that Deutsche faced lower lending yields, tighter competition, flattening loan demand, rising costs and risks entailed in its aggressive expansion into investment banking.

Earlier this week Theodore said Moody's was looking at the implications for Deutsche's ratings from the situation at MGAM, where trading in three funds was halted for three days last week due to "irregularities".
